CausalChain: Low-dose radiotherapy → Induction of immunogenic cell death → Release of neoantigens and inflammatory cytokines (e.g., IFN-γ) → Expansion of circulating precursor exhausted CD8⁺ T cells (Texp) in the STIE → Increased recruitment of Texp into the tumor microenvironment (TIME) → PD-1 blockade lifts inhibitory signals → Differentiation into effective cytotoxic T cells → Enhanced antitumor response
Hypothesis: A sequential therapeutic regimen employing low-dose, fractionated radiotherapy to transiently expand precursor exhausted CD8⁺ T cells, followed by PD-1 inhibitor administration, will synergistically convert immunologically ‘cold’ tumors to ‘hot’ and improve overall treatment outcomes in solid tumors such as non‐small cell lung cancer.
Abstract: Recent advances in single‐cell and spatial transcriptomics have uncovered the dynamic interplay between the systemic tumor immune environment (STIE) and the local tumor immune microenvironment (TIME). Radiotherapy is known to induce immunogenic cell death, releasing neoantigens and inflammatory cytokines that prime immune activation systemically. In parallel, a subset of circulating precursor exhausted CD8⁺ T cells (Texp) can serve as a reservoir for antitumor responses when reinvigorated by immune checkpoint blockade. We hypothesize that a sequential treatment regimen, in which low‐dose, fractionated radiotherapy is applied to induce an inflammatory surge and boost Texp expansion followed by PD‐1 inhibitor administration, can improve T cell infiltration into the tumor, convert ‘cold’ tumors into ‘hot’ ones, and thereby enhance treatment efficacy. This strategy can be optimized by monitoring the temporal and spatial dynamics of T cell subsets with single‐cell and spatial transcriptomic analyses.
